rationale: A wins because it keeps the missing proof visible instead of papering it over with market-story glitter. Its line, "Donors, not districts, are paying for the AI tutor headed to 1 million more students," turns the scale number into a real accountability question; B's "while rivals still charge for it" invents a competitive contrast the update never gave it. B has a solid methodology angle, but too many of its other angles need facts it already smuggled into the headline.
gaps_in_A: "What one pilot district saw when students used an AI tutor regularly" is only pitchable if Khan can name a district and put educators on record; the update does not supply that yet.
"The results exist now; they did not exist before" is a little too neat. The update says Khan is publishing first classroom results now, not that no classroom evidence existed privately before.
"Not for national ed-tech desks" on the local-district angle is too restrictive; a national education reporter could use one district as the human lead for the broader rollout.
gaps_in_B: "while rivals still charge for it" is invented. The update gives no competitor pricing, no rival list, and no evidence that this is a paid-versus-free market split.
"paid commercial products versus a large donor-funded free entrant" repeats the same unsupported market-structure claim. That is not category creation; that is a whiteboard with no sources.
"teachers already stretched thin" imports a teacher-burnout frame the update never supplied. Common-sense context is not evidence.
"which tends to center on students" invents prior Khanmigo coverage patterns. If you need media-history proof to make the angle work, do not state it as fact.
Calling a local-news angle on "which 30 districts are getting Khanmigo" a "duplicate" is wrong. With named districts, that could be the most practical reporting path.
